projects.title: GlanceMap
projects.subtitle:
Follow the lesson.
Find your place again.
projects.description: An AR interface for understanding and remembering audio lessons while walking.

meta.label: Project record
meta.value: July 2025–present · Second author · CHI 2027 submission in progress

hero.alt: GlanceMap pairs a growing mind map with illustrations while the listener walks.
hero.caption: GlanceMap in use. The lesson shown is example study material.

sections.title: A mind map that grows with the audio.
body: While walking, learners look away to check the path. The audio keeps playing, and they can lose the connection between ideas.

GlanceMap pairs illustrations with a growing mind map. Earlier ideas stay visible, so listeners can find their place again. In a study with 16 people, it improved recall immediately and seven days later.

sections.title: Learning on the go means looking away.
body: AR glasses, a walking route, and a podcast that keeps playing. Causes, conditions and comparisons are hard to recover once the explanation has moved on.
Full captions preserve the words, but reading competes with watching the path. How can an AR interface help people attend to their surroundings and follow the explanation when they glance back?

figures.alt: Three moments along the walking route, with the crossing and pedestrian signal.
figures.caption: Walk and listen. Check the crossing. Return to the lesson.

items.title: Walk + listen
items.body: “I’m following the explanation.” Ideas arrive in sequence. AR glasses and earbuds deliver a podcast that builds one idea on the next.

items.title: Look away
items.body: “Is it safe to cross the road?” Attention shifts to the road. The audio continues.

items.title: Look back
items.body: “How did the podcast get here?” The listener missed how the ideas connect and must rejoin the current topic.

sections.title: Could fewer words help?
body: I refined 14 pilots across three rounds. The first round covered pilots 1–3 and 13 cumulative participants.
We tried full captions and isolated keywords. Less text still needed context and the right timing. One learner relied on listening when the keywords did not explain the connections.

figures.caption: Full captions preserve the wording, but require reading.
Naïve keywords reduce text but can lose the links between ideas.

quote.text: no need to show full transcription

sections.title: Could visuals help?
body: Round 2 covered pilots 4–9 and 27 cumulative participants. We tried structured keywords and an Illustration Only interface.
Pictures were quick to grasp. Words still needed clear connections. We kept familiar parent–child structure instead of asking learners to decode a new visual code.

figures.caption: Structured keywords tested spatial hierarchy and color.

items.title: Words need relationships
items.body: “I know each word, but not what they mean together.” — Pilot 8 participant · translated

items.title: Pictures need a brief look
items.body: “I only need a glance or two.” — Pilot 8 participant · translated

sections.title: How much should stay?
body: Round 3 covered pilots 10–14 and 24 cumulative participants. We compared a full logic map with a partial map.
Showing everything created clutter. Removing earlier branches took away the route back. We kept completed branches readable while revealing new ideas with the audio.

figures.caption: Full logic map: more context, but more to search.
Partial logic map: less clutter, but earlier context disappears.

items.title: Recovering an earlier idea
items.body: “I forgot what it had said.” “I used the mind map to help me recall what I had heard.” — Pilot 10 · Participant 2 · translated

sections.title: Six goals, one final design.
body: New ideas appear with the audio. Earlier branches stay readable for a returning glance. Brief labels and familiar branches make relationships easy to read.
The map explains relationships. Illustrations ground concrete ideas. The comparison kept the narration, illustrations and timing the same; the integrated interface added the persistent map.
The three pilot rounds led to six design goals. Their participant counts are cumulative within each round, not a count of unique people across all pilots.

figures.alt: GlanceMap’s final interface, connected by the three original dashed leaders to design goals one through six.
figures.caption: Reveal and retain context; keep labels and links clear; pair relationships with illustrations.

items.title: 01 · Keep text brief
items.body: Use short phrases, not full sentences.

items.title: 02 · Keep ideas connected
items.body: Keep relationships visible.

items.title: 03 · Use familiar structure
items.body: Use parent–child links, with no new code to learn.

items.title: 04 · Ground concrete ideas
items.body: Use pictures for objects and scenes.

items.title: 05 · Reveal with the audio
items.body: Add nodes as the narration unfolds.

items.title: 06 · Help learners return
items.body: Keep past branches readable.

sections.title: Building on illustration-based audio learning.
body: Our Illustration Only prototype used audio-synchronized pictures, informed by the AudioXtend approach. An AudioXtend co-author joined the GlanceMap project.

In the earlier AudioXtend study, 12 participants learned while walking and folding laundry. Audio plus illustrations improved immediate free recall by 33.3% and seven-day free recall by 32.7% over audio alone. These are results from prior work, not GlanceMap.

figures.caption: Our AudioXtend-inspired baseline. This is not a direct test of the AudioXtend system.

items.title: Prior work
items.body: Tan et al. · AudioXtend · CHI 2024.

sections.title: The study, on one shared route.
body: Sixteen participants tried both prototypes. Each heard four lessons, with two lessons per format, in counterbalanced trials. Each lesson lasted 4:55 minutes on average.
Participants completed immediate recall, image recognition and experience measures after each lesson. A remote follow-up repeated recall seven days later.

Meta Quest Pro provided color passthrough and eye tracking. Participants wore earbuds and a right-ankle IMU. A researcher shadowed each trial. The indoor setting limited lighting changes while turns and level changes still demanded attention.
The route created real shifts between learning and navigation. Participants described using earlier branches to recover the explanation, while pictures clarified unfamiliar concepts.

figures.alt: walking-route map, with six numbered markers and the author’s green route annotations.
figures.caption: Walk six indoor laps, take the escalator up, descend the stairs, and rejoin the loop.

figures.alt: masked photograph of the participant walking indoors with Quest Pro.
figures.caption: 01 · Indoor loop. Walk six laps, then change levels. Meta Quest Pro and earbuds deliver the lesson.

figures.alt: masked photograph of the escalator ascent.
figures.caption: 02 · Escalator up. Listen while moving between levels.

figures.alt: masked photograph of the stair descent.
figures.caption: 03 · Stairs down. Watch each step, then rejoin the loop.

items.title: Movement
items.body: Right-ankle IMU recorded walking motion.

items.title: Attention
items.body: Eye-tracking logs recorded viewing behavior.

items.title: What this comparison tests
items.body: It evaluates the complete interface. It does not isolate the effects of maps, persistence or timing.

items.title: Earlier ideas stayed available
items.body: “the earlier part doesn’t disappear; it is one complete thing” — Participant 15 · interview. Earlier branches linked past ideas to the ongoing narration.

items.title: Pictures clarified unfamiliar concepts
items.body: “when it got to a concept I didn’t understand, or some obscure term.” — Participant 08 · interview.

items.title: A returning glance became a review
items.body: “a bit like reviewing.” — Participant 08 · interview. P08 returned to earlier nodes after navigating the route.

items.title: Text helped recover context
items.body: “reading the text is quicker and easier than listening.” — Participant 04 · interview.

sections.title: Better recall, with attention redistributed.
body: Immediate free recall rose from 48.3% to 57.9%. Seven-day recall rose from 45.0% to 52.0%. These material-adjusted gains were 9.6 and 7.0 percentage points.
Picture recognition fell from 83.0% to 75.9%, a loss of 7.1 percentage points. Listeners spent less time on illustrations. They rated the lesson structure 1.59 points higher on a seven-point scale.

Workload showed a modest increase that depended on the model. We found no detectable format effect on gait; this does not prove equivalence. Gaze measures supported returning to the interface, but did not measure recovery time for individual nodes.

items.title: What remains open
items.body: Test individual features, recovery after interruption, outdoor conditions and broader participant groups.

figures.caption: Immediate and seven-day free recall.

figures.alt: Image recognition results for both formats
figures.caption: Picture recognition declined when the map was added.

sections.title: Remember the structure. Give pictures enough room.
body: The recall benefit lasted beyond the walk. Better memory for the lesson came with poorer picture memory. The next design step is to balance these two kinds of information.

items.title: Keep relationships visible
items.body: Use short labels and explicit links.

items.title: Reveal, then retain
items.body: Add ideas with the audio. Keep earlier branches accessible.

items.title: Test visual balance
items.body: Give key images room and adapt detail to the walk.

comic.title: Starting with screen color rules
comic.caption: Alex designs AR UIs. She uses color rules made for screens.
comic.alt: Alex at a desk, designing colored icons on a desktop screen
paragraphs: She uses color rules made for screens.

sections.title: Clear. Comfortable. Meaningful.
body: We tested 12 representative colors. The clearest pairings were not always the most comfortable. We then added icons, and some clear color pairs suggested the wrong meaning.
The guide helps designers choose shadows, outlines or gray backgrounds for alerts, everyday controls and status updates.

sections.title: Screen contrast alone cannot predict AR clarity.
body: On a screen, colors sit on a solid background. AR glasses add the real-world scene. Black becomes transparent, and white can glare.
A color pairing must be checked through the glasses: can people see it, is it comfortable to look at, and does its color fit the icon’s meaning?

comic.title: Trying the UI through AR glasses
comic.caption: Then she tries the UI through AR glasses. “Too much glare.” “Hard to see.” “The color feels wrong.”
comic.alt: Alex wears AR glasses outdoors. The light-bulb, file and bar icons show glare, poor visibility and a misleading color
paragraphs: Then she tries the UI through AR glasses.
“Too much glare.” “Hard to see.” “The color feels wrong.”

items.title: Clarity
items.body: Easy to see.

items.title: Comfort
items.body: Easy on the eyes.

items.title: Meaning
items.body: The color fits the icon.

sections.title: The same people. Two lighting conditions.
body: The same 20 people completed all three studies. XREAL Air 2 Pro was used for the main experiments. HoloLens 2 provided a check with different display optics.

Indoor tests used 250–300 lux; outdoor tests used 1,500–2,000 lux. Lux measures light falling on the surroundings. Participants took a 15-minute break between settings, with two weeks between studies. We collected ratings and explanations.

figures.caption: Indoor experiment · 250–300 lux.
Outdoor experiment · 1,500–2,000 lux.

sections.title: Study 1 · Compare colors.
body: We used 12 representative hues from prior work: 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°, 135°, 180°, 195°, 240°, 270°, 285°, 315° and 345°. These mark positions on the color wheel, not equally spaced steps.
Each background had black, white and opposite-color letters, giving 36 pairs. The letter, size and stroke stayed fixed. Only the colors changed.
Opposite colors often looked clear. White often felt more comfortable. Clarity and comfort could favor different pairs.

figures.alt: The fixed letter T in black, white and opposite color.
figures.caption: The letter, size and stroke stay fixed. Only the colors change.

sections.title: Study 2 · Add meaning.
body: Eight designers proposed icons independently, then agreed on one for each color. This workshop was separate from the 20-person study group.
The twelve functions were dining, finance, light bulb, cycling, video, weather, files, parking, yoga, bar, music and alert.
We retested the same 36 pairs with meaningful icons. Clear color pairs could still suggest the wrong meaning.
Opposite-color icons averaged 4.39/5 for clarity and 2.75/5 for color meaning across all 12 colors. Being easy to see did not guarantee that the color fitted the icon.

figures.alt: The twelve workshop-selected functions, each paired with its color.
figures.caption: Eight designers agreed on one icon per color. The same 36 color pairs were then tested with these icons.

figures.alt: Clarity, comfort and semantic fit ratings
figures.caption: Ratings across three measures with 95% confidence intervals.

items.title: Check meaning as well as visibility
items.body: A color choice can draw attention while sending the wrong message.

sections.title: Study 3 · Refine and retest.
body: We tested workshop ideas for the icon edge and background. We rated clarity, comfort and meaning again, and also asked how strongly each icon stood out.
White icons with a shadow were easiest to notice. Clarity rose by 0.88–1.62 points on a 1–5 scale across four tested colors.
Colored icons with an outline improved the color-meaning rating from 3.71 to 4.13 out of 5, compared with the original black-symbol designs.
A gray background at 30% brightness was least distracting and had the most consistent comfort. This means brightness, not transparency.

figures.alt: The designer workshop and its two refinement sequences: shadow and gradient; outline and gray background.
figures.caption: Workshop ideas became new edges and backgrounds, then returned to testing in AR.

sections.title: Match the design to urgency.
body: Choose how urgently the icon needs to get noticed. Keep the intended meaning while adjusting the edge, outline and background.

comic.title: Applying the AR guidelines
comic.caption: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.
comic.alt: Alex walks outdoors with refined alert, music, dining, weather and file icons in her AR view
paragraphs: With these AR guidelines, Alex can design clear, comfortable icons with meaning that makes sense.

figures.caption: Urgent alerts: white icon + shadow. For information that needs attention now.
Everyday controls: colored icon + outline. Keep functions easy to recognize.
Status updates: colored icon + gray background. Keep information on screen with less distraction.

items.title: Urgent alerts · White icon + shadow
items.body: Use a strong edge for information that needs attention now.

items.title: Everyday controls · Colored icon + outline
items.body: Keep functions easy to recognize, while revealing more of the scene.

items.title: Status updates · Colored icon + gray background
items.body: Keep information available on screen with less distraction, using a gray background at 30% brightness.

sections.title: A gradient can change the message.
body: The symbol can stay the same while a blend looks like a new color. A brighter end can dominate and change what the color suggests.

In the tested cyan comparison, cyan + green was less clear than plain cyan, while cyan + blue was clearer. These examples used ±30° shifts on the color wheel; the stated clarity comparison applies to cyan.
Keep both ends similarly bright, then check through the glasses that the blended color still fits the icon’s meaning.

figures.alt: cyan-green, plain cyan and cyan-blue examples with their observed clarity labels.
figures.caption: For cyan: cyan + green was less clear; plain cyan was the baseline; cyan + blue was clearer. Tested hue shifts were ±30°.

sections.title: Meaning depends on the audience.
body: Some participants read the bar and music colors as youthful and stylish. Would other audiences read them the same way?

The current evidence covers 20 adults and static 2D icons, with East and Southeast Asian design input. Next steps are to test across cultures, ages and visual abilities, explore moving and 3D icons, and use eye tracking to check attention.

figures.caption: Some participants found these bar and music colors youthful and stylish. Opposite colors were not always a poor fit.

projects.title: Color in Context
projects.subtitle:
A color carries
a story.
projects.description: A research-led website for choosing traditional Chinese colors through their origins, cultural meanings and historical context.

meta.label: Progression
meta.value: ColoGene → Color Atlas → future Color Agent

hero.alt: The complete atlas of 48 traditional colors, grouped by origin.
hero.caption: 48 colors · four origin categories: mineral, plant, nature and literary.

sections.title: From a beautiful swatch to a defensible choice.
body: A color carries more than a value. It can signal status and symbolism, record a pigment or material source, and refer to a particular time and place.

We co-designed a website with practicing designers. ColoGene put context beside each color. Interviews and design trials then shaped Color Atlas, which connects 48 colors and recommends five-color palettes. A future Color Agent explores applying and refining those palettes through dialogue.

items.title: Version 1 · ColoGene
items.body: 12 formative interviews and a 10-person pilot. CHI 2026 Poster accepted.

items.title: Version 2 · Color Atlas
items.body: 48 colors, four origin categories, and 25 designers interviewed. Ongoing research.

items.title: Version 3 · Color Agent
items.body: A future design mockup for applying, comparing and refining a palette.

sections.title: What makes a color belong?
body: Debate over museum merchandise colors raised a question: how do designers judge cultural fit? Traditional Chinese colors have material origins, histories and meanings, but the information is scattered.

We interviewed 12 Chinese designers of museum products and historical websites. The semi-structured interviews lasted 30–45 minutes. We asked how they found references, compared palettes and explained their choices.

items.title: Does it fit my historical brief?
items.body: Designers often sample appealing colors from images. The references rarely explain historical use, symbolism or material origins. “A color may represent different things in different cultures.” “…whether this color existed in that historical context.” Show meaning, origin and period beside the color value.

items.title: Which reference can I trust?
items.body: “But the colors people share are not really consistent.” “But I rarely look up where those names come from.” Two websites list Zhu sha as #CA3433 and #9D2933. Connect names and values to traceable historical sources.

items.title: How do I build a whole palette?
items.body: “I’m torn over which colors to use.” “I usually make several versions and then pick the one that looks best.” Designers need complete palettes with a clear cultural rationale.

quote.text: I usually make several versions and then pick the one that looks best.

figures.alt: P13 period storyboard, made using the usual workflow.
figures.caption: P13 · usual workflow. The storyboard shows why a color reference needs a historical context.

figures.alt: curated packaging artifact shown in the Figma research section.
figures.caption: P17 · packaging with Atlas. Colors connect the visual direction to cultural references.

sections.title: Five ways into color knowledge.
body: Three interview insights shaped five ways to explore color knowledge: name origins, hue, color family, dynasty and scene palettes.

Designers knew color names but rarely checked their origins. They used reference images before explaining their choices, and compared palettes mostly by appearance. ColoGene brings the missing context into each step.

items.title: Make meaning visible
items.body: Name origins connect colors to materials, meanings and naming stories.

items.title: Browse with context
items.body: Hue, family and dynasty provide different entry points for narrowing a design direction.

items.title: Compare whole palettes
items.body: Scene-based collections offer three- or five-color combinations.

figures.caption: Make meaning visible. Name origins connect colors to materials, meanings and naming stories.
Browse with context. Hue, family and dynasty narrow the choice by period.
Compare whole palettes. Cultural scenes offer three- or five-color combinations.

sections.title: Promising signals from a small pilot.
body: Ten designers worked on matched Jiangnan and Tang templates. Five used ColoGene; five used their usual workflow. We compared their written reasoning and questionnaire scores.

All five ColoGene users finished within 15 minutes. One of five baseline users did not. Mean questionnaire gains were 8.66 points with ColoGene and 1.21 with the usual workflow, a difference of 7.45 points.

These are early descriptive results from five people per group. Designers reported more confidence in their choices and cultural explanations. They also wanted fuller sources and palettes tailored to their own brief.

items.title: What changed
items.body: Participants could connect color selection to explicit cultural explanations.

items.title: What was still missing
items.body: Fixed palettes and short stories did not cover the complexity of every design task.

quote.text: With ColoGene, I can filter by Tang and see where colors come from.

sections.title: A connected route from brief to palette.
body: Color Atlas organizes 48 colors by origin: mineral, plant, nature and literary. These categories include pigments, dyes, natural imagery and written records.
Hovering a color reveals shared family, period, region and craft relationships. Designers can compare colors through these connections as well as hue.

sections.title: Read the color’s complete record.
body: Click a color to open its information card. The record connects a name and value with its origin, cultural context, historical era and classical references.
Tianqing · #6E9CB3. Its origin describes the sky clearing after rain. The card associates it with Ru-ware glaze and the Five Dynasties to Northern Song period.
The listed classical references are Guide to the Study of Antiquities and Miscellaneous Records of Qingbo. Check the source record before choosing a color.

sections.title: From a brief to five colors.
body: Describe the brief, then compare the recommendation. Preset instructions match the brief against the color database. Each record describes a color’s meaning, history and relationships.
For “Serene Song-ceramic branding,” the example combines sky blue, teal and pale neutrals for a calm ceramic mood. Check the rationale, values and source texts before choosing.

sections.title: Different choices, with context to discuss.
body: Twenty-five designers explored Version 2. They worked on three artworks with their usual workflow and three with the atlas. The design artifacts show how their color direction changed.
The session included a 10-minute pre-interview, 45 minutes with the baseline, 45 minutes with Atlas, a 20-minute post-interview and a 10-minute questionnaire.
Post-interviews asked for more palette directions, fuller sources and selection reasons, support for every object in a complex brief, and more freedom to refine suggestions.

sections.title: A Color Agent that keeps the designer in control.
body: Version 3 is a future design mockup. It has not been implemented or evaluated as a Color Agent. Six implications from Version 2 feedback shape an iterative conversation.

In the palace-magnet scenario, the designer asks for a calm, contemporary Qing-era Beijing palette. The agent compares a warmer direction with a blue-led direction, explains the sources, previews the whole drawing and waits for the designer to refine or accept.

figures.alt: The proposed Color Agent conversation, with six numbered links to research feedback.
figures.caption: A proposed interaction: clarify the brief, compare directions, inspect sources, preview the whole drawing, then refine or accept.

steps.title: Clarify the brief
steps.body: “I’m truly torn over which colors to use.” — P23. Turn uncertainty into a clearer design intention.

steps.title: Set the context
steps.body: “Then I wonder whether this color existed in that historical context.” — P13. Ask for period and place before recommending colors.

steps.title: Compare palettes
steps.body: “It could give me a few more palettes to refer to, so I have more choices.” — P16. Offer distinct palettes shaped by the same brief.

steps.title: Explain the choices
steps.body: “For the stories and sources, I suggest adding a citation.” — P14. Explain meanings and link them to cited records.

steps.title: Apply to every part
steps.body: “Some of the other elements get ignored.” — P25. Preview the palette across all objects in the drawing.

steps.title: Keep judgment
steps.body: “It feels like compromising the design for this color.” — P16. Let the designer refine details or accept the result.

projects.title: PersonaMail
projects.subtitle: Making communication intent editable.
projects.description: People repeat their relationship, tone, and wording preferences for similar emails. PersonaMail remembers useful context and lets writers change one section at a time.
projects.meta: IUI Companion ’26 · March 2026 · Published demo · 2nd author

sections.title: When a similar request returns.
body: You decline a senior colleague’s dinner invitation. You work out a respectful, concise reply. Weeks later, a similar request arrives.

items.title: With general AI
items.body: You explain the relationship and your writing preferences all over again.

items.title: With PersonaMail
items.body: Saved context and wording preferences provide a starting point. You add the new request, tone, and desired length.

sections.title: Evidence informed the prototype.
body: Eight participants tried MailMaestro, Friday Email, and Textoshop. The formative sessions revealed three recurring barriers.
A review of 97 social-psychology papers informed the communication-factor taxonomy.

items.title: Explain the social goal
items.body: Writers found nuanced relationship and situation needs hard to put into a prompt.

items.title: Control one section
items.body: Writers needed an option between rewriting the whole draft and changing individual words.

items.title: Reuse what worked
items.body: Successful strategies had to be recreated when similar situations returned.

sections.title: Remember preferences. Keep the writer in control.
body: How can AI remember useful writing preferences while keeping each new email under the writer’s control?
Saved context is a starting point. Writers can change the situation, tone, length, and intent of each section.

items.title: Make social context explicit
items.body: Choose the relationship and situation. Add details that preset choices miss.

items.title: Keep edits local
items.body: Change the purpose of one section while keeping the rest of the email.

items.title: Carry useful choices forward
items.body: Saved anchors reuse context in similar emails. Edits and optional explanations refine the personal stylebook.

sections.title: Keep the reason private.
body: In the paper’s demonstration, a writer withdraws from a previously accepted dinner invitation from a senior colleague.
They select the justification and change a detailed explanation to a vague or private reason. Only that section changes. The rest of the email stays in place.
The writer can save the successful strategy as an anchor for a future email.
sections.sourceOrigin: Visible portfolio example, supplemented by the published demonstration paper.

sections.title: A personal writing agent.
body: A future personal agent could remember your wording, tone, and recurring context. You would add new details, review the draft, and send it.
This is a potential application. The portfolio demonstrates reusable context and section-level intent editing.

sections.title: Communication preferences that carry forward.
body: Reusable context and a personal stylebook bring communication preferences into future emails. Section-level intent controls keep edits local. Explanations help the assistant learn from those edits.
This published demonstration reports formative findings and a working prototype. It does not report comparative effectiveness results.

projects.title: Beyond the Gaze
projects.subtitle: Looking is only part of the story.
projects.description: A long look does not tell us what a detail means to a viewer. We compare gaze with the regions people later select and explain.
projects.meta: ACM Multimedia Asia 2026 · Accepted · 15–18 Dec 2026 · Co-first author

sections.title: Three signals. The same region.
body: Gaze–Selection–Language compares what a viewer looks at, later selects, and uses to explain a painting.
HLL means High Gaze, Low Selection, and Low Language within the same region. Attention is high, but that region is not later selected or used in the coded interpretation.

items.title: 01 / Region map
items.body: Compare the same semantic region across gaze, later selection, and spoken explanations.

items.title: 02 / Gaze heatmap
items.body: See where gaze accumulated. The heatmap alone cannot explain what a detail means to the viewer.

items.title: 03 / HLL example
items.body: For some viewers, the outlined A5 region drew gaze but was not selected or used to explain the painting.

sections.title: View freely. Recall. Explain.
body: We enrolled 15 participants and analyzed 12 after gaze-quality checks. They viewed 24 Western oil paintings, with five to seven semantic regions in each.
After free viewing, the artwork was hidden. Participants recalled meaningful regions and explained the painting. Questionnaires and interviews followed.

figures.alt: Figure 2 · Twenty-four self-paced viewing, recall, and interpretation trials.
figures.caption: Figure 2 · Twenty-four self-paced viewing, recall, and interpretation trials.
figures.sourceOrigin: Original project paper figure; retained native pixels and source composition.

sections.title: A recurring mismatch.
body: HLL appeared in 156 of 1,651 cleaned participant–painting–region records: 9.4%. All 12 analyzed viewers and all 24 paintings had at least one HLL record.

items.title: RQ1 / How common is HLL?
items.body: It appeared across every analyzed viewer and painting.

items.title: RQ2 / What characterizes these regions?
items.body: In selected examples, they linked foreground and background or sat at transitions in depth.

items.title: RQ3 / How does attention accumulate?
items.body: Selected records showed repeated visits without uniformly long fixations.

sections.title: More returns. Shorter fixations.
body: One participant’s viewing of The Hay Wain provides a concrete example. Region A3 received 38 visits, compared with a trial mean of 20.33.
Mean fixation duration was 0.051 seconds, compared with a trial mean of 0.17 seconds. These values describe one participant, painting, and region.

figures.alt: Figure 5 · One participant–painting–region example, with the original comparison table.
figures.caption: Figure 5 · One participant–painting–region example, with the original comparison table.
figures.sourceOrigin: Original project paper figure; retained native pixels and source composition.

sections.sourceOrigin: Original paper Figure 5; exact native data-visual replacement retained.

sections.title: Attention is one part of interpretation.
body: We compare what viewers look at with what they use to explain a painting. Attention alone cannot tell us which details support their interpretation.
Museum guides could combine gaze and visitor feedback to suggest details worth exploring. This is a potential application, not an evaluated museum intervention.
The study is exploratory. Recall depends on memory and expression. HLL does not prove that a viewer made no interpretation, and the selected examples do not establish a general spatial rule.

sections.title: Connect details to a historical city.
body: 191 survey responses and 30 interviews shaped the design. People could see local details but struggled to locate them within the whole scroll and explain their cultural meaning.

items.title: RQ1 / What blocks understanding?
items.body: A detail can be visible without its place or cultural meaning being clear.

items.title: RQ2 / How can details reconnect?

items.title: RQ3 / What changes with ScrollVerse?
items.body: Understanding ratings were higher. Usability and workload differences were not significant.

sections.title: Compare two ways of viewing.
body: We randomly assigned 60 participants to ScrollVerse or an annotation viewer, with 30 in each group. Questionnaires and interviews followed.
25 of 30 ScrollVerse participants said everyday life in Qing-dynasty Suzhou was easier to understand. This was reported understanding, not a knowledge test.
26 of 30 would recommend ScrollVerse or try similar digital heritage experiences. This describes their intentions after the experience.

sections.title: Keep cultural explanations tied to the painting.

projects.title: VerseColor
projects.subtitle: Follow a color into a poem.
projects.description: A search for “green” finds poems. VerseColor connects colors with imagery, emotions, and original lines so readers can explore what the color means in context.
projects.meta: iConference · Under review · Sep 2026 · corresponding author

sections.title: Follow a connection back to its source.
body: An expert-reviewed graph connects colors, imagery, emotions, and source poems. Readers can follow a color–imagery link back to the poem, then compare how another poet uses that color.

items.title: RQ1 / How do readers construct meaning?
items.body: Readers need the poem’s context, but supporting evidence is scattered across sources.

items.title: RQ2 / How can a graph help?
items.body: Bring color, imagery, emotion, and source lines together. Support comparison across poems and poets.

items.title: RQ3 / Does it help readers interpret poems?
items.body: Readers rated VerseColor more helpful for interpretation. The widely used poetry website was easier to use.

figures.alt: Colors, imagery, emotions, and poetic lines are linked in the VerseColor interface.
figures.caption: Colors, imagery, emotions, and poetic lines are linked in the VerseColor interface.
figures.sourceOrigin: Current visible Figma portfolio; 4× export, 13 October 2026

sections.title: Read the color in context.
body: This example uses Wang Wei’s farewell poem. “Green” describes fresh willows. The following lines supply the farewell between friends.
Select a reading below to trace the connection back to the line.

sections.title: Compare interpretation experiences.
body: Eight reader interviews informed the design. A separate group of eight experts reviewed the graph.
In a 30-participant study, we compared VerseColor with Souyun, a widely used Chinese poetry website. Participants completed interpretation tasks, questionnaires, and interviews.

figures.alt: Study procedure for the comparative interpretation tasks.
figures.caption: Study procedure for the comparative interpretation tasks.
figures.sourceOrigin: Original project paper figure; retained native pixels and source composition.

sections.title: Connecting ideas. Interpreting imagery.
body: Readers rated VerseColor more helpful for connecting colors with imagery and emotion, with Cohen’s d = 2.29. They also rated it more helpful for understanding imagery associated with a color, with d = 1.91.
Cohen’s d describes the size of the rating gap. A larger value means a bigger difference between the tools.
Souyun was easier to use. Ratings for finding relevant poems were similar.

figures.alt: Figure 4 · Original questionnaire comparison chart and study photographs; axes and legend preserved.
figures.caption: Figure 4 · Original questionnaire comparison chart and study photographs; axes and legend preserved.

dataVisual.title: Stronger support for making connections
dataVisual.description: Two reported standardized differences between VerseColor and Souyun.
dataVisual.scope: Cohen’s d is an effect size, not a percentage, multiplier, or learning score. Souyun received higher usability ratings; retrieval-precision ratings were broadly comparable. Short-term questionnaire ratings do not establish durable learning gains.

figures.sourceOrigin: Original project paper figure; retained native pixels and source composition.

sections.title: Traceable interpretation. Easier navigation next.
body: VerseColor links colors, imagery, emotions, and source poems in one place. Users rated it helpful for interpreting poems. The next step is to make navigation easier.
The results describe short-term questionnaire ratings. They do not show objective or lasting learning gains. Expert-reviewed associations do not mean that a color has one universal meaning.

projects.title: Her Sound Re-sound
projects.subtitle: Who gets to tell her story?
projects.description: Waner was a poet and court official; Taiping shaped court politics. Later accounts reduced their lives to scandal and rivalry. Reconstruct their stories, watch them disappear, and reclaim the power to narrate.

hero.alt: Waner and Taiping in the game artwork
hero.caption: Reclaim their past. Imagine our future.

sections.title: Imagine our future.
sections.body:
Created at Beijing’s 1,000-participant women’s hackathon, the game encourages more women to enter STEM and become developers.

Experience the story before questioning the record.

items.title: Two political lives
items.body: Waner drafted imperial edicts. Taiping, daughter of China’s first female emperor, shaped court politics.

items.title: Audience Choice Award
items.body: Awarded at the hackathon.

items.title: Audience feedback
items.quote: We felt the strength of women here. We saw such thoughtful ideas, and wanted to make games of our own.

sections.title: Build a shared memory.
sections.body: Waner and Taiping travel, share a banquet, and remember their time together in poetry. Rebuild these three scenes with five reusable icons.

sections.title: Scroll to watch history disappear.
sections.body: Six chapters become eighteen scenes. As you scroll, eight scenes dissolve while ten remain. The gaps make the loss of their stories visible.

sections.title: Their lives become accusations.
sections.body:
The Old and New Books of Tang tied Waner’s influence to sexual misconduct. The court-commissioned Comprehensive Mirror accused Taiping of acting “to prolong her power.” Later retellings made them romantic rivals.

The game questions history written by victors and men in power.
